title: IRIS Handles 70% of Greek Instant Payments as EuroPA Links Expand
snippet: Greece's IRIS network processed 126.4m transactions worth €10.9bn in 2025, and is now connected to three European A2A schemes via EuroPA. The post IRIS Handles 70% of Greek Instant Payments as EuroPA Links Expand appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Greece’s IRIS payment network now handles around 70% of the country’s instant payment volume, according to a whitepaper published jointly by DIAS S.A., the national interbank clearing operator, and Capgemini Invent. The figures, drawn from 2025 data, place IRIS among the most widely adopted account-to-account (A2A) schemes in Europe by domestic penetration.

Interbank transaction volumes on IRIS grew sixty-fold in five years, from 1.6 million in 2020 to 95.4 million in 2025. The user base expanded from roughly 500,000 in early 2020 to 4.75 million today. On the merchant side, IRIS Commerce recorded 12.4 million transactions worth approximately €4.76 billion in 2025, across around 1.2 million point-of-sale terminals and 70,000 e-commerce outlets.

Cross-border connections through EuroPA

Since 30 June 2026, IRIS has been linked via EuroPA to three European mobile payment schemes: MB WAY in Portugal, BANCOMAT Pay in Italy, and Bizum in Spain and Andorra. The combined network reaches more than 57 million users and allows instant cross-border transfers using a mobile number as the payment identifier, removing the need for an IBAN on the sender’s side.

A further layer of European integration is taking shape. On 30 September 2026, five major European payment schemes, including Bizum, EPI Company’s Wero, SIBS-MB WAY and Vipps MobilePay, announced the formation of the European Network for Payments (ENP), a joint entity designed to operate a shared interoperability hub. DIAS is expected to bring IRIS into ENP. The rollout is planned to begin with cross-border person-to-person transfers before extending to e-commerce and point-of-sale.

Stavroula Kampouridou, chief executive of DIAS S.A., said: “The next challenge is to turn universal availability into active preference at both online and physical points of sale, and to leverage the Greek experience to further develop cross-border instant payments in Europe.”

Market context and regulatory read-across

The IRIS trajectory is significant precisely because domestic A2A adoption at scale remains rare in Europe. The UK’s Faster Payments infrastructure has high transaction volumes but lacks a single consumer-facing brand of comparable recognition. The Netherlands’ iDEAL is well-established in e-commerce but is not a P2P-first product. What IRIS demonstrates is that a utility-layer interbank scheme can be repositioned as a consumer payment brand when accompanied by a coordinated push across participating banks and a deliberate focus on user experience.

The broader European interoperability effort also intersects with the EU’s payment strategy. The European Commission has been explicit in its support for a pan-European A2A alternative to card networks, and PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation currently progressing through the EU legislative cycle are designed to make open-payment infrastructure easier to build on. ENP’s formation, and IRIS’s anticipated participation, places Greek payments infrastructure closer to the centre of that political and commercial project than its size might suggest.

The whitepaper’s own findings point to the remaining gap: IRIS Commerce’s merchant adoption, while growing, has not yet reached the point where A2A is the default checkout option for Greek consumers. Fewer checkout steps, a more consistent experience across banking apps and greater visibility of IRIS at the point of sale are identified as the priorities for the next phase.

The full data in the whitepaper distinguish between interbank and on-us transactions; the headline 70% penetration figure includes both where stated.

title: Allica Bank Passes £100m Interest Milestone for SME Accounts
snippet: The challenger bank says high-street rivals offer an average 0.80% AER on instant-access business deposits, against its own standard rate of 2 The post Allica Bank Passes £100m Interest Milestone for SME Accounts appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Allica Bank has paid more than £100 million in interest through the Savings Pots attached to its Business Rewards Account, the challenger bank announced on 2 November 2026. More than half of that total was paid in 2026 alone, reflecting the rapid growth of an account that launched only in 2023.

Richard Davies, CEO of Allica Bank

The milestone is accompanied by a pointed piece of competitive framing. Allica’s own analysis of six major high-street providers, based on publicly available rates as of September 2026 and using a £75,000 deposit as a benchmark, found that the average instant-access business savings rate across Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Nationwide and Santander stood at 0.80% AER. Allica’s standard Savings Pot rate is 2.83% AER, with a maximum advertised rate of 4.08% AER available to eligible customers who meet behavioural conditions including a minimum number of outbound transfers per month and a full account switch via the Current Account Switch Service.

The Business Rewards Account is designed for businesses with between 5 and 250 employees and bundles the savings product with card cashback, accounting software integrations, team expense cards and dedicated relationship manager support. The number of businesses using the account grew 133% in 2025 to more than 14,000, a figure Allica cites as evidence of broadening demand for alternatives to incumbent business banking.

Chief executive Richard Davies said established businesses had been receiving poor terms on their cash from the larger banks for too long. “Paying our customers more than £100 million in interest from their Savings Pots shows what’s possible when you build a bank specifically to support established businesses,” he said. “This is real money going back into the hands of businesses who are such a critical part of the UK economy.”

The SME savings gap in context

The structural argument Allica is making is not new, but it is gaining traction. A 2024 Allica report estimated that UK SMEs were foregoing up to £9 billion a year in potential interest by leaving cash in low- or zero-rate current accounts, a finding consistent with Bank of England data showing large balances parked in transactional accounts throughout the high-rate cycle that began in 2022.

The competitive dynamic has intensified as the rate environment begins to ease. The Bank of England has moved the base rate downward from its 2023 peak, which has started to compress challenger bank deposit margins while incumbent rates remain low. For Allica, the window in which a meaningful rate gap can be marketed is narrowing, which makes the £100 million figure a timely piece of positioning as much as a milestone.

Regulatory and market backdrop

Allica holds a full UK banking licence, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the PRA and the FCA, which gives its Savings Pot deposits Financial Services Compensation Scheme protection up to £85,000 per depositor. This distinguishes it from some embedded-finance savings wrappers that route deposits through a licensed partner bank, an arrangement that can create ambiguity over deposit protection that sophisticated SME treasurers increasingly scrutinise.

The broader SME banking market remains a regulatory priority. The FCA and Payment Systems Regulator have both monitored access to and pricing of business banking services, and the Competition and Markets Authority’s legacy remedies from its 2016 retail banking investigation continue to shape how challenger banks can market switching incentives. Allica’s use of CASS as a rate trigger is notable in that context: it directly incentivises the switching behaviour the CMA intended to promote.

With total customer deposits now above £5.7 billion and cumulative lending exceeding £3.7 billion, Allica has moved well beyond the scale at which challenger banks typically remain niche. The next milestone that will matter to the market is whether it can sustain deposit growth and margin discipline as rates continue to drift lower.

title: Payment Device Security Can’t be Someone Else’s Problem
snippet: PCA Cyber Security's Gianfranco Vinucci argues certification is only the start, and payment devices need a clear security owner for their whole working life. The post Payment Device Security Can’t be Someone Else’s Problem appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Card terminals and self-service tills stay in the field for years after they are certified, while software, threats and regulation move on around them. A payment security specialist argues that responsibility for those devices is spread so thinly across the industry that nobody owns the outcome, and that payment service providers are best placed to change that.

Gianfranco Vinucci, chief operating officer at PCA Cyber Security

Gianfranco Vinucci is chief operating officer at PCA Cyber Security. In this contributed piece he sets out why payment device security has to be managed across a device’s whole life, not just at the point of certification. The views are his own.

Card payments accounted for 64 per cent of all payments in the UK last year. Most of us do not think twice when we tap a card or phone to make a purchase, and as cash continues to decline we are becoming ever more dependent on payment devices to keep transactions moving.

Whether it is a supermarket checkout, a self-service terminal or the card machine in a local coffee shop, those devices now sit at the centre of everyday commerce. They are no longer background infrastructure; they are part of the critical systems that keep retailers trading, customers moving and payments flowing.

But who is responsible for a payment device five years after it has been deployed?

Payment devices commonly remain in service for seven to ten years. During that time, software changes, vulnerabilities emerge and new threats appear, while the environment around the devices keeps evolving. The payments industry has spent years building strong foundations for device security. The challenge now is making sure those devices stay secure long after they enter service.

The challenge starts after certification

A device may meet every requirement when it is certified, at launch, during major updates and periodically depending on the regulations in place. That does not mean it remains secure years later, between certifications, once software updates, configuration changes and newly discovered vulnerabilities have altered the environment it operates in.

Certification is an essential starting point, but it captures a device at one moment in time. The security challenge begins when the device enters the field and starts operating across different merchants, networks and software environments.

The volume of vulnerabilities being discovered should concern every organisation that operates connected devices. In 2021, around 20,000 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) were published. Last year there were more than 50,000, across all technology rather than payments alone. At the same time, AI is speeding up how quickly vulnerabilities can be found and exploited.

Payment devices are also becoming more sophisticated, evolving into connected, software-driven platforms rather than simple pieces of hardware that only process transactions. If the industry focuses only on whether a device was secure at the point of approval, it risks missing how quickly that position can change once the device is deployed.

That is why ongoing assurance needs more than static checks: continuous vulnerability monitoring, periodic penetration testing, real-world attack simulation and clear evidence that devices remain secure as threats, software and operating environments change. Organisations need to know what has been deployed, how devices are configured and where action is needed when new risks emerge.

The set-and-forget problem

Large retailers often have sophisticated fleet management systems that help them keep track of thousands of devices. Much of the SME market does not. Smaller merchants may have fewer internal resources, less technical support and less visibility over whether a device is running the latest approved software or configuration.

A device might still be compliant on paper, but that is not the same as knowing its current security posture. This is where the set-and-forget problem is most acute: once a device is installed and working, it is easy to assume it needs no attention until something breaks or a new requirement forces a change.

Part of the difficulty is that payment device security sits across several organisations. Manufacturers build and certify devices. Payment service providers (PSPs) manage services and customer relationships. Merchants operate the devices. Standards bodies define the requirements. Everyone owns a piece of the process, but it is far less clear who owns the security outcome over the full lifecycle.

When vulnerabilities emerge, responsibility often follows contractual boundaries. That is understandable, but vulnerabilities exist regardless of which organisation owns which document. The industry needs greater clarity on ongoing ownership, visibility and lifecycle management, because device security cannot be passed between stakeholders once a device is in the field.

New obligations under the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) will put more pressure on manufacturers selling into the European market to report actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products. Those obligations could collide with the reality that many manufacturers do not yet have mature processes for monitoring how criminals target vulnerabilities in deployed devices, or the intelligence needed to detect exploitation quickly. That includes visibility of dark web forums, where vulnerability discovery and exploitation can develop before the risks are widely understood.

Why PSPs will matter more

PSPs already manage large device estates, maintain customer relationships and have a strong incentive to understand what is deployed in their environments. Many have invested heavily in fleet management because they recognise the value of operational visibility. That gives them a practical role in connecting compliance, deployment and day-to-day security management.

To work out which devices are affected by a newly identified vulnerability, which software versions are running and where action is needed, organisations first need a clear view of what has actually been deployed. Without it, even a well-understood vulnerability becomes hard to manage across a fragmented estate. Being able to validate, or even recreate, the software bills of materials (SBOMs) that suppliers provide matters more than ever.

This is one reason PSPs are becoming central to the lifecycle security conversation. They sit closer to deployed device estates than most other stakeholders, already run many of the processes needed to maintain visibility over time, and are well placed to make sure security information moves between the parties involved rather than staying trapped in separate contractual or operational silos. The next step is bringing security and fleet management closer together, so visibility is treated as part of how device security is managed rather than as a separate operational concern.

That does not mean PSPs should carry all the responsibility. Effective security will always need collaboration between manufacturers, PSPs, merchants and standards bodies. But lifecycle security needs a clearer operational home than it often has today. As payment devices become more connected and stay in use for longer, the question is no longer simply whether a device was secure when it was certified. It is whether the industry can prove it remains secure in the field, every day it is used.

New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities.

  

            						

The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services.

Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing.

Developed in partnership with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and technology partner NayaOne, the Observatory helps meet the growing demand for greater visibility of AI adoption across the sector.

The resource highlights a range of AI use cases shaping financial services, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI.

By widening access to market intelligence, the Observatory will help firms of all sizes learn from developments across the market, better understand emerging technologies and make more informed decisions about adopting AI responsibly. 

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'AI is creating significant opportunities across financial services, and we’re committed to helping firms understand how the technology is being used.

'The AI Spotlight Observatory provides an open and accessible resource that brings together real-world examples of AI adoption, helping firms, innovators and researchers learn from developments across the sector and identify new opportunities for innovation and growth.'

Notes to editors

The FCA’s AI Spotlight Observatory is the first resource of its kind for a regulator globally.  

It builds on the FCA’s AI Spotlight Digital Showcase, a repository of practical AI solutions across specific themes, by adding new features and capabilities, such as a common taxonomy for comparison, a distinction between use cases and implementations, and the ability to identify emerging patterns across the market. 

The platform is open and accessible to all users. Registration is required to access more detailed insights, such as target client information, and to request demonstrations directly from innovators featured on the platform. 

The Observatory will continue to evolve through the addition of new use cases. Firms can apply to be showcased on the platform.

CFTE has supported the development of the Observatory across three main areas: creating the taxonomy, building the repository, and socialising the Observatory with the market.  

The Observatory forms part of CFTE’s wider collaboration with the FCA on AI capability, industry engagement and market intelligence. Alongside initiatives such as the Agentic Academy, CFTE supports the FCA in helping the financial-services sector better understand, structure and respond to the opportunities and challenges created by AI. 

NayaOne has been responsible for the design and development of the Observatory platform, including the user interface, navigation, search and filtering capabilities. 

The platform builds on the FCA’s wider work on AI, including its  

AI Discussion Paper, AI Sprint, and AI Lab, which includes AI Live Testing and its groundbreaking Supercharged Sandbox supported by NVIDIA, NayaOne and Anthropic. 

Last month, the FCA published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services.

title: Mashreq Puts NEO BIZ and its Fintech Partnerships on Show at Expand North Star 2026
snippet: The UAE bank heads to Expand North Star intent on hearing where founders still hit friction, and on showing how its business banking, AI work and partner network are built to remove it. The post Mashreq Puts NEO BIZ and its Fintech Partnerships on Show at Expand North Star 2026 appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Banks are not always the first names founders look for at a startup show, but Mashreq sees Expand North Star as exactly the right room. Ahead of this year’s event, The Fintech Times looked at what the bank is bringing to the expo floor and what it wants to come away with.

Listening for friction

Mashreq’s stated aim is to meet founders, investors, corporates and technology partners, pinpoint the points of friction businesses still face, and work out how practical digital-first banking and stronger ecosystem partnerships can address them at each stage of growth. The bank says earlier conversations of this kind have already shaped how it serves entrepreneurs. Its view is that while the UAE offers one of the world’s most dynamic environments for starting a business, founders still face hard decisions on financial readiness, operational efficiency and long-term growth, and that the bank’s job is to take some of that weight off them.

It is equally keen to build relationships with investors, corporates and technology partners that share its focus on practical solutions, as those links matter more as businesses scale into new markets.

Banking at the speed of business

The centrepiece will be the full NEO BIZ proposition, built around the idea that banking should be seamless enough for entrepreneurs to concentrate on running their companies. A headline feature is the One-Day Service Promise, which allows eligible entrepreneurs to open a business account within a single day.

Beyond onboarding, Mashreq will show its award-winning business banking app, which gives owners visibility and control over payments and foreign currency transactions, and its Value-Added Services Platform, which offers curated business applications covering accounting, payroll, cybersecurity and productivity. For companies needing more tailored support, a dedicated team of trade, FX and insurance advisers helps with international transactions and financial risk.

From set-up to scale

The bank draws a clear line between the needs of a new business and those of a scaling one. For startups, one of the first and most stubborn hurdles is the time, complexity and paperwork involved in opening a business account, and delays there can hold up paying suppliers, hiring staff or serving the first customers. As companies grow, the focus moves to day-to-day operations, cash flow and having the right financing in place, while fragmented processes and poor visibility over cash can quietly slow growth.

Mashreq’s response combines the reworked account-opening journey through NEO BIZ, digital tools for managing finances and a full range of business banking, lending included. It also stresses financial readiness: the right banking relationship, enough liquidity and planning for changing conditions matter as much to a company’s resilience as securing funding.

The funding picture

The bank links the UAE’s rise as an entrepreneurship hub to initiatives such as the UAE National Innovation Strategy and the Dubai Economic Agenda D33. Recent figures back that up: MENA startups raised USD 1.65 billion across 145 deals between July and September 2026, with USD 507 million across 41 deals in the UAE alone.

Even so, Mashreq notes that finding the right capital at the right stage remains difficult for many businesses, and believes banks can do more by going beyond conventional lending through partnerships and closer engagement with the startup community. Its NeoVentures arm, which supports fintech innovation and capital needs, is its vehicle for doing so. The bank also argues that the funding conversation now has to include resilience, balancing growth ambitions with disciplined cash flow and liquidity management so that capital is deployed well once raised.

AI across the bank

Mashreq is embedding AI across the business with three priorities: efficiency, security and a smoother customer journey. API integrations with the Dubai Unified Licence and Emirates Facial Recognition already simplify digital KYC and onboarding. Internally, an agentic AI pilot with IBM is aimed at simplifying integration engineering, and generative AI capabilities added to its fraud management platform with Clari5 are designed to sharpen detection and speed up investigations.

Looking ahead, the bank expects AI’s biggest impact to be more intuitive, personalised banking, with staff freed to focus on higher-value work that needs human judgement, while customer trust, security and responsible deployment remain non-negotiable.

Fintechs as partners

Fernando Morillo, group head of retail banking at Mashreq

Mashreq increasingly treats fintechs as partners rather than rivals, pairing their speed and technical skill with its infrastructure, regulatory experience and scale. It sees the biggest opportunity in embedding banking within platforms businesses already use, from payment providers to accounting software.

Raj Tatavarty, head of products & digital, business banking at Mashreq

That is already visible in its partnerships. Work with Toothpick and Cashew brings financing into customer journeys, a tie-up with HAL, a B2B platform, helps SMEs to find their next buyer and supplier, partnership with Sukoon lets SMEs buy insurance through digital banking, and a partnership with NEO PAY offers POS and payment gateway services at preferred rates within the NEO BIZ onboarding journey. For the bank, the partnerships that count are the ones that solve practical problems and make financial services easier to reach.

Mashreq frames its presence at the event around a broader point: startups and technology companies are central to the UAE’s economic diversification, and banks can no longer act in a purely transactional way. It wants to work alongside founders, investors, government entities and fintechs, and sees Expand North Star as a platform for those conversations, both in the UAE and further afield.

At the show

Fernando Morillo, Group Head of Retail Banking, and Raj Tatavarty, Head of Products & Digital, Business Banking, will represent Mashreq at Expand North Star 2026 and are available for further information on the bank’s plans for entrepreneurs and the startup ecosystem. Expand North Star 2026 opens with the GITEX Summit at Dubai World Trade Centre on 7 December, before the startup exhibition runs at Dubai Exhibition Centre, Expo City Dubai, from 8 to 10 December. The Fintech Times is a media partner of the event.

title: SFF 2026: Monzo’s Secret for Growth, and the Tokenisation of Global Trade
snippet: Georgia Hanias rounds off Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 with Monzo CEO TS Anil's lessons on leadership and growth, plus the future of tokenised trade finance. The post SFF 2026: Monzo’s Secret for Growth, and the Tokenisation of Global Trade appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 closed out with a fantastic fireside chat featuring Monzo CEO, TS Anil. This was an interesting choice, given the event was in Asia – a part of the world with no shortage of regional heavyweights to spotlight. 

The fact that organisers selected a UK success story to take centre stage underscores that London still remains a global powerhouse for nurturing and scaling amazing fintechs.

The conversation offered a candid look at how hard it is to sustain business growth, and how resilience and strong company culture can serve as a vital defence shield against crisis and create a blueprint for modern banking. It also provided practical lessons for entrepreneurs trying to stand out and lead in an increasingly crowded market.

Weeks of runway, zero room for error

Anil took the helm of Monzo during Covid’s early weeks when the bank had just weeks of capital left. Survival demanded a chain reaction: fix regulatory controls for three million customers to earn regulator trust, unlock shipping velocity to restore investor confidence, and secure the right talent. The North Star? “Make money work for everyone.” The strategy? A 100-day sprint with one rule: avoid decision paralysis. Get through it.

“Let’s not get overwhelmed by the size of the problem.,” Anil told the audience. “Don’t freeze. Just don’t take no for an answer, or be dogged in the pursuit of stuff that needs to get done, and own the whole damn thing.”

Product strategy: the power of ‘not yet’

Monzo’s vision – one regulated platform for all money needs -from lending to saving and investing – required knowing what to build and what to skip. For example, when launching wealth products, the team deliberately said no to crypto, calling it FOMO-driven rather than thesis-based. The principle: refuse to monetise “customer ignorance, inertia, or vulnerability.” Build only what’s genuinely good for customers.

Mission meets business plan

Scaling meant pairing Silicon Valley velocity with banking compliance while protecting Monzo’s culture. The result? Two-thirds of Monzo’s one million new UK customers each quarter come via word of mouth. Reviews use “love” seven times more than competitor banks.

“A mission without a business plan is a frickin’ bumper sticker. How do you create a mission that’s congruent with a business plan – in a way that they are a force multiplier for each other?”

Anil’s track record answers that question. Now the plan is global expansion – with a plan to adapt its tech and customer-first mindset to local regulatory needs. I am sure millions more customers will continue to fall in love with this bank. It will be a grand love affair without borders, because Monzo is truly one of fintech’s greats. The real deal, as they say.

Connecting capital to commerce: tokenising supply chain finance

Elsewhere at the festival, the conversation shifted from consumer banking to global trade – another sector ripe for fintech disruption.

During a panel at the NEC booth moderated by Suresh Neelakantan, head of innovation and development, digital finance at NEC APAC, and featuring Madhivanan Periannan, CEO of TasConnect and Kailash Madan, chief commercial officer at Triple-A, explored how tokenisation is pushing supply chain finance beyond digitisation into programmable, multi-lender ecosystems.

Digital platforms moved trade away from paper, but Neelakantan noted that digitising data means nothing unless it unlocks commercial value. For Periannan, tokenisation turns static trade documents into investable assets:

“What we have done as part of digitising supply chain finance is to ease the financing option – moving away from paper-based financing to digitalised financing. Now, what does tokenisation mean to us? We are digitising the asset itself, which creates a potential opportunity for multiple markets to finance that asset.”

Traditional supply chain finance traps corporate buyers in rigid bank credit lines with narrow lender pools carrying all the risk. Converting contracts and receivables into fractionalised, on-chain tokens with verified data opens access to non-bank lenders, private investors, and alternative liquidity – especially for complex cross-border deals.

Critically, on-chain receivables solve duplicate financing – where exporters pledge the same invoice to multiple funders.

Madan explained blockchain’s role as built-in safeguard: “The beauty of the blockchain is that it is transparent, open, and irreversible. Once an underlying asset has moved on-chain and received funding from one source, other funders can easily see that it has already been financed – which eliminates duplicate funding in the vast majority of cases.”

Tokenised securitisation – bundling trade receivables for institutional investors – remains on the horizon. Both panellists acknowledged the ecosystem hasn’t fully embraced this yet, with foundational rails like tokenised bank deposits still working through interoperability blockers stopping mainstream institutional adoption.

This will take time. But as Monzo proves, pairing real-world utility with relentless execution turns roadblocks into growth engines. With fintech and DeFi converging, the industry’s future is bright.

title: Oraseya Capital Arrives at Expand North Star 2026 with a Bigger Cheque Book and a Wider Mandate
snippet: Fresh from doubling its fund to AED 1 billion, the venture arm of Dubai Integrated Economic Zones (DIEZ) heads to Expand North Star looking for UAE founders, international companies choosing Dubai and, above all, co-investors. The post Oraseya Capital Arrives at Expand North Star 2026 with a Bigger Cheque Book and a Wider Mandate appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
When Expand North Star returns this December, one of the busiest investors in the UAE will be telling a slightly different story to the one it told a year ago. Oraseya Capital, the investment arm of DIEZ, which brings together Dubai Silicon Oasis, Dubai Airport Freezone and Dubai CommerCity, has spent the past three years writing Pre seed- Series B cheques in companies with a pre- existing tie to the UAE. Ahead of the show, The Fintech Times looked at what the firm wants to achieve on the expo floor, and the answer is that it now intends to stay with its founders for much longer.

Phase II in practice

In October, DIEZ doubled the size of the fund from AED 500 million to AED 1 billion, lifted the maximum investment per company to USD 6 million and extended the mandate to beyond Series Band international companies that have relevance to the objectives of the UAE. The news is already public, so there is no fresh announcement planned for the event. Instead, Oraseya sees Expand North Star as its first major ecosystem moment since the increase, and the place to explain what this second phase means day to day: larger tickets, support that continues as companies mature, and a fund able to follow its strongest founders into their next markets.

Pre-Seed remains part of the picture. What changes is that the firm can now also take part in larger rounds, back companies beyond Series B and invest in overseas businesses with strategic relevance to the UAE.

Who Oraseya wants to meet

The firm has three groups in its sights. The first is founders building from the UAE, from idea stage through to growth. The second is international companies who have already setup or are considering to set up their regional base in Dubai, particularly in Oraseya’s priority sectors of healthcare and longevity, fintech, digital assets and artificial intelligence. The third, and the one it regards as most important, is co-investors. Its view is that the strongest rounds are built with partners, and Expand North Star brings an unusually dense concentration of global investors to the city across three days.

A track record built on deal flow

Oraseya launched in November 2023 and now holds 66 active portfolio companies, adding roughly 25 new investments a year. MAGNiTT ranked it the most active investor in the UAE by deal count in 2024, 2025 and the first half of 2026, and second most active across MENA in H1 2026. The firm was also named Venture Capital Firm of the Year at the Entrepreneur Middle East Awards 2025, and the fund increase came less than three years after launch.

What it looks for in a founder

The firm’s approach puts the founder ahead of the business plan. It looks for clear thinking, quick execution and intellectual honesty: people who know their numbers, are open about what they do not yet know, and learn faster than their market moves. Conviction counts, but so does the ability to hire people better than themselves.

Oraseya is wary of headline metrics. It conducts thorough due diligence covering areas ranging from commercial, financial and technical exercises and pays attention to  second order metrics such as retention and repeat usage than to downloads, whether unit economics strengthen rather than weaken as a company grows, and to whether customers would genuinely miss a product if it vanished. One question comes up early in every conversation: can the company win beyond the UAE? Dubai makes an excellent launchpad, in the firm’s view, but category leaders are designed for regional or global markets from the start.

Reading the funding market

Oraseya points to MAGNiTT data showing that MENA funding over the first nine months of 2026 held up far better than deal count, which fell by a third, while early-stage activity dropped to its lowest level in a decade. Capital has not left the region; it has concentrated in fewer, larger rounds, and the UAE attracted two-thirds of all MENA funding in the first half of the year.

The firm sees the best opportunities where the region has a structural advantage. In fintech, segments from SME lending to payments remain underserved. In healthcare and longevity, the UAE pairs policy ambition with purchasing power and fast adoption. Digital assets benefit from one of the clearest regulatory frameworks anywhere. In AI, Oraseya favours companies that turn the technology into measurable revenue for a defined customer, and it says it stays disciplined on valuation.

The pressure points sit at both ends. Fewer cheques at the earliest stage thin out the pipeline of future Series A companies, while growth rounds that fund expansion into several markets remain hard to raise, and fragmented regulation across the region makes scaling dearer than in a single large market. That is the reasoning behind both its continued early investing through its SANDBOX programme and the move beyond Series B: founders should not have to look elsewhere at the point they need most support.

Dubai as a launchpad

For Oraseya, Dubai’s case rests on fast technology adoption, a location within a few hours’ flight of the GCC, Africa, South Asia and Europe, and a government that acts as both early customer and long-term partner. Full foreign ownership in free zones, no personal income tax and visa routes that help attract senior talent complete the picture. Through the DIEZ zones, founders can license, hire, raise and find first customers within one ecosystem, and the firm argues that the real question for the best of them is how far they intend to go from Dubai.

It also sees a wider role for investors than writing cheques. UAE startups aiming to become global businesses need follow-on capital that lasts beyond Seed, introductions to customers and co-investors in new markets, and governance that meets international standards before it is demanded of them. The international mandate is designed to open doors abroad for UAE founders and to bring strong overseas companies into Dubai.

Julien Plouzeau, senior partner at Oraseya Capital

Expand North Star complements that work. With international participation in regional rounds having dipped, the event puts global investors, corporates and talent in front of UAE founders on home ground. Oraseya measures its value in the months that follow, when a meeting turns into a term sheet or a pilot becomes a market entry, which is why it backs the event.

At the show

Julien Plouzeau, Senior Partner at Oraseya Capital, will be at Expand North Star 2026 and is available for further information on the fund’s Phase II strategy and its plans for the region. Expand North Star 2026 opens with the GITEX Summit at Dubai World Trade Centre on 7 December, before the startup exhibition runs at Dubai Exhibition Centre, Expo City Dubai, from 8 to 10 December. The Fintech Times is a media partner of the event.

The Bank of England (the Bank), Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Payment Systems Regulator (PSR) have completed their annual review of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on payments.

  

            						

Read the MoU (PDF)

Outcome of the review:  

The review found that cooperation and coordination between the Authorities – the Bank, FCA, PRA and PSR – has strengthened and remains effective.

We concluded that no changes to the MoU are needed at this time.

To complement the MoU, we have updated our information explaining how our objectives, regulatory remits and key workstreams fit together.

The Authorities have considered the effectiveness and efficiency of their coordination under the MoU. This includes feedback from industry and regulated firms to determine whether the MoU’s principles of coordination and cooperation continue to be met in practice.  

The review found that cooperation and coordination remain effective, with respondents welcoming tangible progress in how the Authorities work together. Examples of this include collaborating on a range of developments, including the future regime for dual-regulated stablecoin issuers and other innovations in payments, including the work of the Payments Vision Delivery Committee.

Following the review, the Authorities have concluded that no changes to the MoU are needed at this time.  

The Authorities have provided further updates to the information detailing each Authority’s regulatory remit and will continue working together to identify areas where greater coordination would benefit the industry.  

This will help firms navigate the regulatory landscape and support a more coordinated and effective approach to payments regulation. This approach is further embedded through the Government’s decision to consolidate the PSR into the FCA, meaning greater coordination, clearer responsibilities and a simpler experience for firms.

fullText:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at TheCityUK National Conference 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: TheCityUK National Conference 2026, Bristol

Delivered: 19 November 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 7 minutes

Highlights

The UK is a global leader in fintech, but we cannot take that position for granted. Firms and regulators alike have to challenge established thinking, embrace uncertainty and try new approaches.

We are changing how we work to keep pace with innovation. That means challenging existing processes, embracing new technology and working with firms to find better ways of doing things.

We encourage firms to come to us early with their ideas. Our Innovation Services are there to help you navigate regulation, test new ideas safely and bring responsible innovation to market.

It’s hard not to feel inspired in a city like Bristol, with its rich history of innovation. 

First, it was aeronautics. Then, it was microchips. Now, it’s fintech. 

Bristol is home to nearly half of all fintech firms in the South West.

Clusters like this one don’t just happen. 

They’re built by people willing to challenge established thinking and take a chance on something new.  

That takes courage.

But for innovation and growth to really thrive, regulators have to be willing to do the same.  

That carries risk. But so does sticking to what we know.  

    

              

How we got here

            						

Our willingness to do things differently in this country has helped make our financial services sector one of the most innovative in the world.

We didn’t get here by accident. 

It took ambitious firms, given the right amount of room to experiment.

The FCA recognised the importance of pushing the boundaries with Project Innovate in 2014.

And the world’s first Regulatory Sandbox in 2016, allowing firms to test innovative ideas with dedicated FCA support.

By 2024, fintech was the most significant job source in UK financial services.

Fintech firms contribute positively to growth, productivity and infrastructure.

No wonder the UK is Europe’s top spot for fintech investment.

But we can’t take that position for granted.

Investment is down. Global competition is up. Funding is getting harder to come by.

And operational disruption is no longer a matter of if, but when.

We’ve recently seen the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange robbed of more than $6 billion.

And a global tech outage that left millions of employees without the tools they need to do their jobs.

Market integrity risks have never been greater.

That's not a reason to hold back on innovation.

If anything, it’s a reason to keep going. We can’t solve these challenges if we stand still. 

But we need to be clear-eyed along the way.

That doesn’t mean certain.

None of us can wait for perfect information.

You decide whether to build, hire or invest before knowing if the idea will work.

We often need to decide whether to act – and how – without the full picture.

Uncertainty comes with the territory.

And in a rapidly changing world, we need to be comfortable making decisions in the face of it.

The decisions that got us here were made that way. The ones ahead will be too. 

          

              

Regulation, growth and innovation  

            						

People often ask how regulation supports growth and innovation.  

But what about regulators?  

Our job is to make sure this sector grows and innovates in ways that create better outcomes for consumers, businesses and the wider economy.  

That means writing rules and working differently: being faster, more accessible, more willing to listen.

And backing experimentation through our Innovation Services, where we help firms navigate regulation and test ideas safely.

We’re seeing results. Firms that enter our Regulatory Sandbox are more likely to raise capital and attract greater investment.

And demand is growing.

We had more applications to the Sandbox and Innovation Pathways in the first half of 2026 than in the whole of 2025 – 92% from firms we haven’t worked with before.

These services are particularly valuable for young firms testing their ideas and business models, with around 70% of applications coming from firms in their first two years.

We’ve scaled and embedded these services across authorisations, policy and supervision. 

Because innovation and regulation are not separate.

          

              

Keeping pace

            						

Markets are changing. So is the speed of innovation.

But so are we. 

Our Innovation Services and the testing they facilitate are faster than sending Q&A between legal and compliance teams, and the regulator.  

And what we learn through experimentation shapes how we regulate and what we share with the market.

You’ve seen this in our approach to artificial intelligence (AI).

Our AI Lab is a place for firms to work with us and explore AI’s potential, risks and opportunities.

It also helps us understand what works.

And today, we’re launching the world-first AI Spotlight Observatory.

Built on cases from over 200 organisations across 150 areas of activity, it shows how firms are really using AI across financial services.  

So you can learn from each other and see where the opportunities lie.

AI could also improve how firms manage risk.

At Mansion House, our chief executive asked whether it’s time to rethink the so-called three lines of defence model: the frontline business, risk and compliance, and internal audit.

I’m taking forward work to explore how innovation could help firms manage risk, grasp opportunities and serve customers better.

That includes better connecting all three lines – with real-time assurance and challenge informed by more timely business insights.

Some firms already use it that way.

Our supervisors are adjusting, too.

As part of being a smarter regulator, we’re modernising how we supervise.

And are looking at whether we ask for duplicative board packs or data that no longer reflects how firms manage risk.

We will also take a step back to understand how firms operate today, and how technology can help us focus on outcomes rather than processes.

Effective risk management is key. 

But it also has to be efficient: timely. Evidenced. Focused on outcomes.

I’ll set out a detailed engagement plan in the coming weeks so we can examine these opportunities together.

Alongside this, our chief operating officer is exploring how to simplify the process around know your customer compliance (KYC).

KYC is an important customer information source, alongside firms’ transaction monitoring, timely investigations of alerts and reporting suspicions.

We know it can feel like the focus is on process over outcomes. 

Now is the time to challenge existing processes and be willing to change what isn’t working. 

If you’re already innovating across your lines of defence or have ideas for simplifying KYC, come and talk to us. 

          

              

Going further 

            						

Our Innovation Services aren’t just for the Next Big Thing. We’re open to any idea that could improve financial services and support growth.

We’re already seeing more firms come forward with ideas.

But we want to hear from firms that haven't used our services much – like those in consumer credit or working on financial inclusion.

That said, not every idea needs our Innovation Services.

Sometimes firms may simply have questions about getting authorised, or the requirements set by various bodies.

That’s why we offer things like our pre-application support service.

And are now letting firms know before authorisation that we’re likely to approve them, helping them secure funding sooner.

We’re committed to working with others to find solutions where a system-wide answer is needed.  

For example, our public statement on safely offering workplace saving schemes, including interactions with our rules and minimum wage requirements.

Our work and our approach reach beyond the UK.

In October, we worked with IOSCO to power its first-ever AI TechSprint, focused on investor education in the age of AI.

Our sandboxes let us test ideas within the existing rules.  

But sometimes the legal framework itself is the barrier. 

Most legislation was written before this kind of technology existed – and it can hold innovation back.

The Digital Securities Sandbox shows what’s possible when rules and legal requirements can be set aside, safely.

It’s a big part of why PISCES, the new private securities market, was up and running so quickly.  

And testing it in the Sandbox means future legislation will be grounded in evidence – not guesswork.

          

              

Take a seat at the table  

            						

There are a lot of conversations happening right now – and there is room for everyone at the table.

So, please, pull up a chair.

We’re making a deliberate effort to get out and hear from stakeholders first-hand.

This year, our executive team alone has made 25 visits across the country.

And we’ve been engaging with consumer groups and firms in Bristol for some time.

Last year, our chief executive met with local fintechs to discuss our strategy and encourage them to use our Innovation Services.

There will be more visits to come.

I know approaching us isn’t always easy.

Too often, firms rule themselves out before they’ve even spoken to us because they don’t have all the answers.

We understand.

But we want to hear from you.

Because while we’re a regulator, we’re also human. And we genuinely want to help.

If you’re innovating, and think your ideas fall within our regulation, come and speak to us.

In return, we’ll listen. Give clear answers. Think differently. And work with others.

Take, for example, agentic AI.

We recently published a joint statement with our partners in the Digital Regulatory Co-operation Forum on protecting people and businesses in an agentic economy.

Because agentic products blur the line between regulated and unregulated activity.

Just because a business describes itself as a technology provider doesn’t mean it can offer financial services without our authorisation.

So, if you're developing or deploying personal agents, come to us early to test your ideas.

We'll move at pace, so responsible innovation can move quickly. 

          

              

Conclusion

            						

The next chapter will be written by those willing to try something new.

Of course, innovation is never without uncertainty. It’s an uncertain world we live in.

Embracing it takes courage – and that’s how we unlock the growth our economy and financial system need.

I doubt those using the Kennet and Avon Canal in the 1800s saw much need for a new way to move people and goods between Bristol and London.

Then came Brunel’s Great Western Railway, which changed everything.

As the most successful entrepreneurs and investors know, sometimes the greatest risk isn’t taking a chance.

It’s standing still.

The state imposed the penalty on Block’s buy now, pay later business after finding the company failed to assess customers’ ability to repay loans.

        

            

        Published Nov. 25, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
        
            Courtesy of Afterpay
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

The California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation imposed a $2.68 million fine on Block’s buy now, pay later Afterpay business after finding that the company didn’t assess customers’ ability to repay loans as required by state law.

The state is taking the enforcement action against Afterpay to protect Californians using BNPL services in the wake of the federal government reversing consumer protection policies, according to a press release the agency issued Tuesday.

“California’s financial watchdog is taking action against Afterpay for illegal lending practices that set borrowers up to fail,” said California Business and Consumer Secretary Rohit Chopra in the release. “While federal regulators are turning a blind eye, California will continue to enforce the law to guard against consumer abuses.”

Dive Insight:

The California agency contended that Afterpay and other BNPL services have a legal obligation to implement basic checks of consumers’ ability to repay loans before extending any financing to them. That would include checking their income and other debts. That legal requirement is a protection to keep borrowers from finding themselves in a downward debt spiral, the state said.

The state agency pointed to Afterpay, which Block agreed to acquire for $29 billion in 2021, as a major BNPL lender and noted that its customers have been increasingly using the financing to buy everyday goods, like grocercies, as inflation pushes prices higher. Block also owned the merchant services company Square as well as the digital wallet services company Cash App.

BNPL services may lead consumers to spend more than they otherwise would, putting them at risk of taking on excessive debt, the state contended. An investigation of the company between January 2020 through March 2022 showed that the company’s failure to properly assess the ability to repay put borrowers at increased risk of default, the release said. 

“DFPI’s investigation found that some of Afterpay’s customers had concerningly high default rates and substantial outstanding debts,” the release said.

In his prior role as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s director, Chopra tried to impose new federal requirements on BNPL financing providers in 2024, seeking to require such financing be subject to the same laws that apply to credit card lending.

The CFPB reversed course on those policy initiatives after President Donald Trump took office last year. Chopra exited his role leading that federal agency in February 2025. Trump officials subsequently undertook significant paring of the agency’s workforce.

The California enforcement action pointed to CFPB research from last year showing 60% of BNPL users had other loans, held high balances on credit lines, and had low credit scores. The federal agency also said younger borrowers were more likely to carry BNPL debt as a higher percentage of their total debt.

Firms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.

They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.

Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.

Innovation is becoming more interconnected

Innovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.

Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.

A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.

Financial inclusion

Firms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.

Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.

A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.

What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over time

We are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.

Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.

We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.

We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.

Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.

Looking ahead

Applications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.

They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.

We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.

The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.

We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.

Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.

Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.

Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.

We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

To find out more about our innovation services and keep up to date with future opportunities, visit our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways pages.

title: Cap One pursues payments modernization
snippet: The bank’s investments in real-time and cloud-based rails are letting it keep pace with technology advances, a top payments executive said.
fullText:
Avik Chatterjee is Capital One Financial’s managing vice president overseeing payments, specifically with responsibilities for the bank’s technology related to enterprise money movement platforms. 

He is also the bank’s divisional chief technology officer for enterprise payments. That includes the infrastructure for card, auto loan and banking business payments as well as managing teams that have purview for payment rails and applications moving money in and out of the bank. 

In an interview late last month, he spoke about how the bank is pursuing the modernization of payments for its corporate clients as it adapts to industry trends, especially the shift toward real-time payments. 

Chatterjee also shared what developments he expects as the bank prepares for the further evolution of payments, including how artificial intelligence is helping combat fraud.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

PAYMENTS DIVE: Given your role, what developments are you watching with respect to stablecoins, agentic commerce and digital wallets?

AVIK CHATTERJEE: Digital currencies [and] stablecoins are definitely interesting new innovations in the space that we find ourselves in, and we're always keeping an eye out on how does that create valuable experiences for our customers, and so my role is to basically provide the solutions as the businesses require them. We serve the different lines of business: retail, commercial, small business, and so, as needs evolve, we are definitely keeping an eye out on the trends.

What other trends are you watching for 2027?

The general theme seems to be, how does banking and money movement keep pace with the needs of the customers in the market that we find ourselves in, and from that perspective, it is definitely a move from more latent rails, like the ACHs and the wires – wires are obviously not as latent depending on the time of day or the day of the week, but from those rails, we are seeing a shift into more real-time based payments.

What is becoming interesting is how can some of these financial institutions and banks be prepared for this move to real-time. If you think about traditional banking operations, there was this notion that you can shut down the money movement rails for a certain time in the day – whether it's the end-of-day activities, maintenance activities, or issues and incidents that happen unbeknownst to us – and that kind of operation does not lend itself into the adoption of real-time applications, or real-time payments.

Avik Chatterjee

How much has the bank invested in modernizing its operations, and has it moved away from the COBOL operations that still are part of some U.S. banks’ infrastructure?

Those COBOL systems and mainframes are alive and kicking in [the industry]. Maybe not kicking, but they're alive. These are complex systems. There are operations built around it…

What I see is modernization investments are being done across all major banks. I think we are further ahead because of our declaration of building all the software within Capital One on the public cloud, which was built natively. For example, the FedNow and the RTP rails that we built are end-to-end on the public cloud on Amazon Web Services infrastructure, which means that they were built in the modern stack itself. We didn't have to migrate any legacy flows to meet these rails. When we talk about ACHs or wires, though, we still have investments to be made. 

So, in my space, I still see there is a difference of maturity in terms of systems that are modernized, [and] systems that are on the path to be modernized. But one of the good things about Capital One is we are always making those investments. 

I, unfortunately, cannot talk about exact dollar values in terms of how much is left versus how much has been done, but suffice to say, it is one of the goals for us to have all the rails, not just the real-time rails, run fully end-to-end on a modern cloud-native infrastructure.  

How are you meeting clients’ needs for artificial intelligence?

We cater to small business and commercial customers, so AI helps lift all boats from that perspective. For example, we have debit cards which my teams manage, launch and run, and there are debit card programs for our retail customers as well as our small business customers. For both of those cohorts of customers, I think where AI helps is fraud detection in the two seconds that we can make a decision on these transactions. We continue to refine our models to make sure that there are less false positives, [and] higher approval rates for the transactions when the customer actually swipes or taps their card.

You raise an important issue, which is fraud. Anything new in particular you're planning with respect to fraud in 2027, like any new approaches related to AI models? 

The industry, and the landscape, are definitely evolving, and so are our fraud models. It takes a while for new patterns to be understood and models to be created against them. The good news is that we have invested a lot in terms of our data infrastructure, which is the foundation on which we can build these new fraud models. We are invested in creating data products, which gives us a very structured, well-managed way of exposing the data layer into the models’ layer. Therefore, we can create these models at a much faster pace by looking at the data trends that we are seeing in the industry.

UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow.

  

            						

The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.

In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.

The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast-evolving threat environment.

It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers.

Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said:  

‘Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance.

‘Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.’

Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said: 

‘Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.’

Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said:

‘We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents.

‘The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.’

Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risks

Separately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing.  

The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions.  

These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area. 

Notes to editors

The FCA, PRA and the Bank have jointly published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management.

The consultation closes on 26 February 2027.

Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year.

The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements.  

The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve.

The proposed guidance key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas include:

Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management, with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance.

Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk, maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts.

Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats, applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains.

Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly, through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks.

Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively, with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned.

The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future.

A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years.

In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI.

title: LO:TECH Raises $12m Series A to Bridge Digital and Tokenised Markets
snippet: The London capital markets firm, backed by MMC, Faction and 13 Books Capital, will use the funds to expand into New York and Singapore. The post LO:TECH Raises $12m Series A to Bridge Digital and Tokenised Markets appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
LO:TECH, a London-based capital markets firm built around round-the-clock and onchain trading infrastructure, has closed a $12 million Series A led by MMC Ventures. Existing backers Faction and 13 Books Capital participated alongside new investor Atka. The company did not disclose a post-money valuation.

The proceeds will fund geographic expansion into the US and Asia-Pacific, with New York and Singapore named as priority locations, and the scaling of execution services for institutional clients. LO:TECH also said it is exploring regulatory licences in the US, a necessary step for any firm seeking to provide execution services to American institutional counterparties under the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission frameworks.

The infrastructure argument

LO:TECH’s proposition rests on a single architectural claim: that its trading systems were designed from scratch for markets that run continuously, across both onchain venues and traditional exchanges, rather than retrofitted from legacy infrastructure built around fixed trading hours. The firm operates across designated market making, market data and execution services and says it serves more than 50 institutional clients, including publicly listed companies.

Chief executive and co-founder Tim Meggs framed the opportunity in structural terms. “Capital markets were built for a world that opened at 8am and closed at 4.30pm. That’s not how risk is traded any more,” he said. “The best trading firms in the world are technologically advanced, but they grew up on top of traditional market infrastructure. We built ours from scratch for markets that run 24/7, onchain and across every asset class.”

The company reports triple-digit revenue growth in each of the past two years, having tripled revenue and doubled headcount since its prior funding round in August 2025. Those figures are unaudited and come from the company’s own release, but they provide context for MMC’s conviction at Series A.

Market context

The timing is deliberate. Total crypto market capitalisation fell roughly 50 per cent in the year to June 2026, according to Chainalysis, and Bitcoin lost around $62,000 from peak to trough over the same period. Capital that retreated from speculative digital assets has not simply exited the broader onchain ecosystem; much of it appears to have rotated into tokenised real-world assets. Data from RWA.xyz cited in the release shows the value of tokenised real-world assets on public blockchains nearly doubled over a similar period, rising from roughly $20.6 billion to $38 billion. Tokenised equities alone grew from approximately $960 million in March to $3.2 billion by late September 2026.

The direction of travel has attracted established market infrastructure operators. In June, Intercontinental Exchange, parent of NYSE, and crypto exchange OKX announced a joint venture to offer OKX customers access to NYSE-listed tokenised equities, subject to regulatory approval. That kind of cross-venue arrangement is precisely the market LO:TECH is positioning itself to service.

The competitive set for institutional crypto and tokenised-asset execution now includes both native digital-asset firms that are adding traditional market capabilities and incumbent prime brokers and market makers that are building or acquiring onchain infrastructure. LO:TECH’s edge, to the extent it can sustain one, lies in the depth of its cross-venue technology and the regulatory licences it acquires as it enters new jurisdictions. The US licence process, in particular, will be a meaningful signal of how seriously the firm is taken by institutional counterparties that operate under strict counterparty risk frameworks.

Ollie Ricards, partner at MMC, noted that the firm has delivered consistent revenue growth through a difficult period for crypto markets, describing LO:TECH as positioned to provide the infrastructure that always-on venues will need as trading volumes in tokenised assets continue to grow.
